Module 7 | Beginner study guide

CNNs and RNNs for Text

Two ways a computer can learn from words: spot nearby patterns, or follow a sentence step by step. Start with the everyday idea, then learn the vocabulary.

Plain-language explanations + real-world examples + memory cues

Start with the big picture

A neural network cannot directly read a sentence. First, text is changed into numbers. Then a model learns which number patterns help with a task, such as sorting a review or finding a person's name.

CNN: the phrase spotter

Looks at short neighboring groups of words, searching for useful local patterns wherever they appear.

Analogy: Scanning a review for a phrase like “stopped working.”

RNN: the running note-taker

Reads one token at a time and carries a changing summary of what it has seen so far.

Analogy: Listening to a story while remembering earlier details.

Real-world choice: To label a whole customer review as positive or negative, a CNN can look for helpful phrases anywhere in it. To label each word in “Maya joined Acme in Paris,” an RNN can use the word order and its running context to identify a person, company, and place.
Text into numbers CNNs RNNs Compare them Course toolbox Self-check

1. Before the network: text becomes numbers

Neural networks do calculations on numbers. A typical text-classification pipeline begins with these steps:

1. Split“Great little camera”
→
2. Tokenizegreat · little · camera
→
3. EncodeTokens become IDs and vectors
→
4. LearnModel predicts a label

Token

A piece of text the model processes, often a word or subword piece.

Token ID

A number used as a label or lookup address for a token. ID 12 is not inherently “more” than ID 4.

Embedding

A list of numbers (a vector) representing a token. It gives the model a learnable way to work with words.

Document matrix

A table of word vectors: one row per token, with rows in sentence order. This is a convenient input shape for a text CNN.

Two encodings in the course: the introductory slides demonstrate one-hot vectors, where each word gets its own mostly-zero row. The toolbox uses an embedding layer, which maps token IDs to denser vectors that the model can learn. Pre-trained embeddings are another option, but the toolbox's embedding layer is learned as part of its model.

Why pad or truncate?

Sentences have different lengths, while a batch is easier to process when examples have a common length. Padding adds placeholder tokens to shorter sequences. Truncation shortens sequences that exceed a chosen limit.

Padding is not a real word. Treat it as a structural placeholder so the model does not learn that extra padding means something. Choose a reasonable maximum length: using the single longest document can waste time and memory.

Cleaning text can help, but do it thoughtfully. The toolbox removes common words and short tokens; for a different task, removing not from “not safe” could erase the most important clue.

2. CNN: look for useful word neighborhoods

A text convolutional neural network (CNN) slides small learned filters over neighboring word vectors. Each filter produces a score that says how strongly a local pattern matches what it has learned.

Think of a search highlighter. In “The delivery was late, but the driver was kind,” a filter might learn to respond to a phrase that helps with a delivery-complaint category. It is a helpful analogy: the model learns numerical patterns from examples; it does not begin with a built-in English dictionary of complaint phrases.

How the filter moves

Imagine each word as a row in a spreadsheet. A text filter covers a few adjacent rows and the complete width of each word vector. It moves along the sentence—not sideways through part of a word vector.

  • A width-2 filter examines two neighboring tokens at a time, like a bigram-sized window.
  • A width-3 filter examines three tokens at a time; wider filters can find longer local patterns.
  • The filter's weights are learned during training and reused at every position. This is called weight sharing.
Number of valid positions = sentence length − filter width + 1

Example: An 8-token sentence with a width-3 filter has 8 − 3 + 1 = 6 possible window positions. A filter evaluates each of those six windows to make a feature map.

From windows to a decision

  1. Convolution: score each local window; the collection of scores is a feature map.
  2. ReLU: a simple activation that turns negative scores into zero while keeping positive scores.
  3. Pooling: keep important responses while shrinking the feature map. Global max pooling keeps the largest response per filter, wherever it appeared.
  4. Combine: join the pooled filter outputs and send them to a dense layer.
  5. Predict: produce category scores or probabilities, such as spam/not spam.
Memory cue: CNN = slide, score, keep the strongest, classify.

Why use a CNN instead of connecting everything?

A fully connected layer gives every input its own connections to later neurons. A CNN uses small windows, reuses the same filter across positions, and can use pooling to reduce the amount of information it carries forward. These choices can reduce complexity and help the model notice a useful phrase wherever it occurs.

One trade-off: global max pooling remembers the strongest response, but not exactly where in the document that response occurred. Also, fewer parameters do not guarantee a model will never overfit.

3. RNN: keep a running summary of the sequence

A recurrent neural network (RNN) processes tokens in order. At each position it combines the current token with a hidden state—a learned, compact summary carried from the preceding step.

Word 1Start a running summary
→
Word 2Update the summary
→
Word 3Use earlier context
→
OutputTag, classify, or predict

For example, when tagging “Maya and Leo work at Northstar in Toronto,” an RNN can carry clues forward as it reads. A sequence-labeling model can produce an output for each word: Maya → PERSON, Northstar → ORGANIZATION, Toronto → LOCATION. Real systems need suitable training examples and may also use information from both directions.

A simplified picture of its repeating step is:

new hidden state = combine(current token, previous hidden state)

The model reuses the same learned weights at every time step. This is parameter sharing through the sequence. The carried state is useful context—not a perfect recording of every earlier word.

Three useful input/output patterns

PatternWhat goes in and comes out?Example
Many-to-oneMany input tokens, one prediction for the sequence.Classify an entire restaurant review as positive or negative.
Many-to-manyA prediction at each step of an input sequence.Tag each word in a sentence with a part of speech or named entity.
One-to-manyOne input, a sequence of outputs.Generate a caption from an image or continue a text prompt.

RNN language model: predict what comes next

A language-modeling RNN can learn to predict the next token from the earlier ones. For “we like NLP,” the training examples include we → like and like → NLP. At generation time, the model predicts a next token, adds it to the sequence, then predicts again.

How does an RNN learn across time?

Training sends prediction errors backward through the repeated steps. This is called backpropagation through time (BPTT). It lets a later mistake affect the earlier steps that helped produce it.

A difficulty for basic RNNs: as learning signals travel through a long sequence, they can become too small (vanishing gradients) or too large (exploding gradients). Exploding gradients can be limited with gradient clipping; gated alternatives such as LSTMs and GRUs are designed to help preserve useful information over longer spans.
Memory cue: RNN = read in order, update memory, produce an output.

4. CNN or RNN? Choose by the job

QuestionCNNRNN
How does it read?Looks at short neighboring windows, often across the sentence in parallel.Reads one step at a time and carries a hidden state.
What is its natural strength?Finding local patterns that can occur in different positions.Using order and earlier context in a sequence.
Example from M7Classifying text, such as a newsgroup post.Tagging each word for named entity recognition.
What should you remember?Pooling can discard where a strong feature was found.A vanilla RNN can struggle to retain information over long distances.

Neither model is automatically best for every language task. The right choice depends on the data, the goal, and the practical constraints. Compare against a simple baseline rather than assuming a bigger or newer model must win.

Fast recall: CNN asks “Which local phrases matter?” RNN asks “What have I read so far?”

5. The course toolbox: from reviews to predictions

The M7 CNN toolbox walks through a real document-classification workflow using a subset of the 20 Newsgroups dataset. Its four example categories cover atheism, religion, computer graphics, and space science.

  1. Inspect the examples: read sample posts and check their category labels.
  2. Prepare the text: clean and tokenize posts, create a vocabulary, map tokens to IDs, and pad or truncate sequences.
  3. Build a CNN: use learned word embeddings and parallel filter widths of 2, 3, and 4 tokens to look for patterns of different lengths.
  4. Classify: global max pooling combines each filter's strongest response; dense layers make the final category prediction.
  5. Evaluate: inspect accuracy, a classification report, and a confusion matrix—not only the training score.
  6. Compare: the toolbox also evaluates a TF-IDF + Naive Bayes baseline on the same categories.
Case-study result: The toolbox lecture reports roughly 89% test accuracy for its CNN and 84% for its Naive Bayes comparison. Those figures describe this particular run and setup; they are not a promise about a new dataset. The confusion matrix also shows that posts about atheism and space can be hard to separate because their vocabulary sometimes overlaps.

Read evaluation like a fair referee

  • Training set: examples the model learns from.
  • Validation set: examples used during development to choose settings or a checkpoint.
  • Test set: held back until the end for a fair final check.

The course notebook is a teaching demonstration. For a rigorous evaluation, keep a separate validation set rather than repeatedly using the test set to choose the best model. Build vocabulary and preprocessing choices from training data, then apply them to validation and test data. A confusion matrix helps show which categories the model mixes up; per-class precision and recall help show performance for each category.

Toolbox setup tip: The original and Colab-updated notebooks contain environment setup and deep-learning library instructions. Software versions can matter, so use the notebook that matches your environment and check its setup before running installation cells.

Quiz memory: The M7 quiz asks which CNN layer reduces the feature-map dimensions. The answer is the pooling layer. Softmax turns output scores into class probabilities; a fully connected layer combines features for a prediction; ReLU adds a non-linear step.

6. One-minute recap

  1. Text becomes tokens, IDs, and vector representations before a network can process it.
  2. A text CNN slides reusable filters over neighboring word vectors to find useful local patterns.
  3. Pooling shrinks feature maps; global max pooling keeps the strongest response per filter.
  4. An RNN reads a sequence in order and passes a hidden state from one step to the next.
  5. Many-to-one can classify a whole review; many-to-many can label every word.
  6. BPTT trains the RNN through its sequence; vanilla RNNs can face vanishing or exploding gradients.
  7. Use held-out evaluation and compare with a baseline before deciding whether a model is useful.
Remember it in one breath: CNN finds local patterns; RNN carries context in order.

7. Quick self-check

Try answering before opening each explanation.

A sentence has 8 tokens. How many valid windows does a width-3 filter see?

Six: 8 − 3 + 1 = 6 possible positions.

What does a text CNN filter cover when it examines three neighboring words?

Three complete neighboring word-vector rows, spanning the embedding dimension. It moves along token positions, not sideways through a partial word vector.

What does global max pooling keep, and what can it lose?

It keeps the strongest response from each filter, but loses the exact location where that response occurred.

Why is an RNN's hidden state useful?

It carries a learned summary of earlier sequence steps into the current step, so the prediction can depend on word order and prior context.

Which model pattern fits one sentiment label for a whole review?

Many-to-one: many word inputs contribute to one document-level output.

What does the pooling layer do in the CNN quiz?

It downsamples the feature maps, reducing their size. Softmax has a different job: turning output scores into class probabilities.

Why should the test set be saved for a final check?

If you repeatedly use test results to choose a model or tune settings, the test set is no longer an independent check of how the model may perform on new data.
